knowledge_point.title: Solving First-Order Initial Value Problems Using Integrating Factors

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\left(1\right)y=6,\quad y(0)=-6
$$

Select the correct options below.

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=6.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int 1\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+1y) & =e^{x}\cdot 6 \\ e^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+e^{x}y & =6 e^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{x}) & =6 e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int 6 e^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{x} & =6\left(1 e^{x}\right)+C \\ ye^{x} & =6 e^{x}+C \\ y & =\left(C + 6 e^{x}\right) e^{- x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=-6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(6 e^{(0)})+C}{(e^{(0)})} \\ -6 & =\frac{6+C}{1} \\ C & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=6 - 12 e^{- x}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=24 x^{2},\quad x>0,\quad y(1)=-6
$$

Select the correct options below.

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The first step is to write the equation in standard form,

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y & =24 x^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x}\left(x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\right) & =\frac{1}{x}\cdot 24 x^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y & =24 x\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=24 x.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int \frac{2}{x}\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{2 \ln{\left(x \right)}} \\  & =x^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=x^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & =x^{2}\cdot 24 x \\ x^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2 xy & =24 x^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx^{2}) & =24 x^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 24 x^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ yx^{2} & =6 x^{4}+C \\ y & =\frac{C + 6 x^{4}}{x^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(1)=-6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =\frac{(6 (1)^{4})+C}{((1)^{2})} \\ -6 & =\frac{6+C}{1} \\ C & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=\frac{6 \left(x^{4} - 2\right)}{x^{2}}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\left(6\right)y=6 x e^{- 6 x},\quad y(0)=6
$$

Select the correct options below.

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=6$ and $Q(x)=6 x e^{- 6 x}.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int 6\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{6 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{6 x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{6 x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y) & =e^{6 x}\cdot 6 x e^{- 6 x} \\ e^{6 x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6 e^{6 x}y & =6 x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{6 x}) & =6 x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{6 x})\,\text{d}x & =\int 6 x\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{6 x} & =3 x^{2}+C \\ y & =\left(C + 3 x^{2}\right) e^{- 6 x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(3 (0)^{2})+C}{(e^{6 (0)})} \\ 6 & =\frac{0+C}{1} \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=3 \left(x^{2} + 2\right) e^{- 6 x}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\left(\frac{x}{5}\right)y=\frac{4 x}{5},\quad y(0)=-6
$$

Select the correct options below.

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{x}{5}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{4 x}{5}.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int \frac{x}{5}\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{5}y) & =e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}\cdot \frac{4 x}{5} \\ e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}}{5}y & =\frac{4 x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}}{5} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}) & =\frac{4 x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u=\frac{x^{2}}{10}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{4 x e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}}{5}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}} & =\int 4e^u\,\text{d}u \\ ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}} & =4e^u+C \\ ye^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}} & =4 e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}+C \\ y & =\left(C + 4 e^{\frac{x^{2}}{10}}\right) e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{10}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=-6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(4 e^{\frac{(0)^{2}}{10}})+C}{(e^{\frac{(0)^{2}}{10}})} \\ -6 & =\frac{4+C}{1} \\ C & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=4 - 10 e^{- \frac{x^{2}}{10}}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\left(\frac{x^{2}}{3}\right)y=\frac{5 x^{2}}{3},\quad y(0)=6
$$

Select the correct options below.

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{3}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{5 x^{2}}{3}.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int \frac{x^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x^{2}}{3}y) & =e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}\cdot \frac{5 x^{2}}{3} \\ e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x^{2} e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}}{3}y & =\frac{5 x^{2} e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}}{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}) & =\frac{5 x^{2} e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u=\frac{x^{3}}{9}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{5 x^{2} e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}}{3}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}} & =\int 5e^u\,\text{d}u \\ ye^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}} & =5e^u+C \\ ye^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}} & =5 e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}+C \\ y & =\left(C + 5 e^{\frac{x^{3}}{9}}\right) e^{- \frac{x^{3}}{9}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(5 e^{\frac{(0)^{3}}{9}})+C}{(e^{\frac{(0)^{3}}{9}})} \\ 6 & =\frac{5+C}{1} \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=5 + e^{- \frac{x^{3}}{9}}.
$$
